question: A 53-year-old man comes to the emergency department for severe left knee pain for the past 8 hours. He describes it as an unbearable, burning pain that woke him up from his sleep. He has been unable to walk since. He has not had any trauma to the knee. Ten months ago, he had an episode of acute pain and swelling of the right great toe that subsided after treatment with indomethacin. He has hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, psoriasis, and hyperlipidemia. Current medications include topical betamethasone, metformin, glipizide, losartan, and simvastatin. Two weeks ago, hydrochlorothiazide was added to his medication regimen to improve blood pressure control. He drinks 1–2 beers daily. He is 170 cm (5 ft 7 in) tall and weighs 110 kg (242 lb); BMI is 38.1 kg/m2. His temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F). Examination shows multiple scaly plaques over his palms and soles. The left knee is erythematous, swollen, and tender; range of motion is limited by pain. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Patient presents with severe left knee pain" -> "History of acute pain and swelling in the right great toe" -> "Suggestive of possible gout" -> "Elevated serum uric acid levels expected" -> "Serum uric acid level test is appropriate" -> 85%

CHAIN: "Patient has erythematous, swollen left knee" -> "Acute inflammatory arthritis suspected" -> "Previous episode of gout indicates possible recurrence" -> "Arthrocentesis can confirm diagnosis and relieve pressure" -> "Most appropriate next step in management" -> 90%

CHAIN: "Patient has fever and swollen knee" -> "Infection or inflammatory process considered" -> "Arthrocentesis can rule out septic arthritis" -> "Fluid analysis can guide treatment" -> "Intra-articular treatment may be needed" -> 80%

CHAIN: "Patient has multiple scaly plaques" -> "Psoriasis may contribute to joint inflammation" -> "Psoriatic arthritis possible" -> "Intra-articular triamcinolone could reduce inflammation" -> "Considered if gout is ruled out" -> 75%

CHAIN: "Patient has a history of gout" -> "Indicates potential for acute gout attack" -> "Colchicine is effective for acute gout" -> "However, diagnosis needs confirmation" -> "Serum uric acid or arthrocentesis preferred first" -> 70%
analysis: The patient's presentation is highly suggestive of acute gout, particularly given his history of a previous episode involving the right great toe, which is a classic location for gout attacks. The severe pain, erythema, and swelling of the left knee, along with the elevated temperature, further support this diagnosis. In acute gout management, the most appropriate next step is to confirm the diagnosis through arthrocentesis, which allows for synovial fluid analysis to check for monosodium urate crystals. While serum uric acid levels can be helpful in the long term management of gout, they are not reliable during an acute attack. Other options like colchicine and intra-articular corticosteroids are also treatments for acute gout, but they are typically initiated after confirming the diagnosis. Therefore, arthrocentesis is the most appropriate next step in management.
